name: Currencies sorted on sovereign credit risk

origin.source_title: Exchange Rates and Sovereign Risk (working paper; published in Management Science 2022)

how_it_works.simple: Use the price of insurance against a country defaulting to choose currencies: riskier countries pay more interest but their currencies tend to fall.
how_it_works.analogy: Like a lender charging a riskier borrower more: the extra interest may or may not cover the chance of losing out.
how_it_works.precise: Della Corte et al.: buying high and selling low sovereign-risk currencies (by exposure to global CDS spreads) earns 6.25% a year, Sharpe 0.71, 2003 to 2013, with forward returns including carry. Calice and Lin: currencies of countries with the highest past CDS spreads have the lowest future spot returns; low-minus-high spread up to 9.4% a year in spot terms, 2007 to 2021.

rule: Monthly: rank currencies by 5-year sovereign CDS spread; the sign of the trade depends on whether carry is included (see the two papers).
economic_rationale: Sovereign risk is a priced global risk in currencies and accounts for a large share of carry returns.
why_it_might_fail: Data is paid; the two papers point in opposite directions once interest is included, so the signal mostly re-labels carry.

reported_results.source: Della Corte, Sarno, Schmeling and Wagner (2013), working paper, Table 6
reported_results.notes: Quote: "Investors earn 6.25% p.a. for buying high and selling low sovereign risk currencies and the corresponding Sharpe ratio is 0.71."

reported_results.source: Calice and Lin (2022), EFMA paper, Table 2
reported_results.notes: Spot returns only; low-minus-high CDS portfolio spread between 3.6% and 5% a year for one-month holding, up to 9.4% in the abstract.

post_publication_evidence: Calice and Lin (2022) confirm the spot effect over 2007 to 2021.

relevance.reason: Interesting for EM, but needs paid data.
